articles.headline: Sean McVay sheds light on Kyren Williams' postgame comments about role
keyFacts: Los Angeles Rams running back Kyren Williams made surprising comments about his role following a loss to the Arizona Cardinals.
Head coach Sean McVay said Monday that Williams explained his postgame remarks and clarified that he only meant to be a spark for the team.
McVay stated that he completely understood Williams' explanation and noted that the player's intentions were misinterpreted.
body: Kyren Williams was understandably frustrated after the Los Angeles Rams ' loss to the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, as was everyone in the team's locker room. He had a decent day, putting up 67 total yards on just 13 touches, but that certainly didn't meet his own expectations.
During a media scrum with reporters, Williams was asked why the Rams are lacking consistency from drive to drive, and his comments turned some heads .
“Can’t tell you, bro. Probably because I’m not out there,” he said.

Sean McVay said on Monday that Williams came to him about his comments and explained what he meant, which the coach "totally understood." McVay says Williams' comments weren't how he intended them to be taken, and that Williams always wants to "be that spark" for the team.

"He brought it up to me. I wasn't aware of it," McVay said. "He's such an energy for us. He was emotional after the game. I know this guy's heart. He wants to make sure that he's influencing and affecting positive change. I think what he said it was more of, ‘I just always want to try to be that spark.’ He was frustrated after the game, but his teammates know what he's about. When he explained it to me, I totally understood where he was coming from. He's a great leader for us. I think the way that it was interpreted was not what his intentions were. I know his teammates and I felt that way. He actually brought that up to me on his own. I was not aware of it until he brought it up to me.”

Williams has always been a team-first player for the Rams, even with his playing time and touches decreasing over the last couple of seasons. Blake Corum has eaten into his role but it's allowed Williams to stay fresh and more efficient when he does get the ball.

The Rams voted Williams a team captain and he's always been a leader in the locker room, which made his comments after the game so surprising. But McVay clarified what the star running back meant and went straight to his coach to explain his intentions.

articles.headline: 'Password1' and a forgotten test account land Welsh outfits in hot water
keyFacts: A ransomware attack compromised the personal data of 3,300 people after an intruder exploited a forgotten test account protected by the password Password1.
The Information Commissioner's Office issued reprimands to Ogi Networks Limited and Data Cymru for security failures related to the breach.
Regulators stated that the two organizations failed to properly maintain accounts or evaluate security measures over a period of more than 12 years.
body: A test account protected by "Password1" helped an intruder steal personal data relating to 3,300 people, mostly children, in a ransomware attack that has drawn regulatory rebukes for two Welsh organizations.
The Information Commission's Office (ICO) issued reprimands rather than fines to Ogi Networks Limited (ONL) and the Local Government Data Unit – Wales, also known as Data Cymru.
According to the ICO, altnet ONL provided server and connectivity infrastructure, licensing, and support to Data Cymru, which helps public bodies across Wales make effective use of data.

On November 1, 2024, Data Cymru suffered a ransomware attack after a miscreant exploited a test account called Test2 to infiltrate its network and encrypt 182.7 GB of data housed in a file server and an internal database server.
"Before deploying the ransomware, the threat actor exfiltrated 42 GB of data from a primary domain controller, a file server and an SQL server," the ICO said on Tuesday in its reprimand of ONL [PDF].
ONL told the ICO it created the test account on January 13, 2012, during its initial project for Data Cymru.

"ONL confirmed that the creation of the 'Test2' account was likely intended to test user account access before migrating 'real' users to its services," the ICO said. "When it was created, the 'Test2' account was given the password of 'Password1'."
The ICO cited Bitwarden's password strength tool, which rated "Password1" as "very weak" and estimated a cracking time of less than a second.

"The local administrator accounts on the three impacted systems all had the same password. This meant that once one system had been breached, the local account hashes could be collected and used by the threat actor to authenticate access to other systems on the Data Cymru network," the regulator added.

"ONL confirmed that it did not carry out any reviews of local administrator accounts following their initial deployment. This meant these accounts remained active, regardless of whether they were used, and continued to use the same default passwords set at the time of their creation in January 2012, as part of ONL's initial project with Data Cymru, for more than 12.5 years."

The data watchdog reprimanded ONL under Article 32 of the UK GDPR because it failed to put in place "appropriate technical and organisational measures" to ensure processing systems and services were safe, and it didn't regularly assess or evaluate those measures. It found ONL had no auditing procedures to review user accounts within Data Cymru's Active Directory.
The ICO's separate reprimand of Data Cymru [PDF] also detailed failures in its security arrangements.

"Password1 is not an appropriate password, it is a wide-open door to nefarious actors," said ICO head of investigations David Doodson. "This incident shows how a single weak password, attached to an account that was no longer needed, can leave the door open to a serious cyber-attack that can affect thousands.

"The responsibility for these failures did not sit with one organisation alone. ONL created the test account whilst Data Cymru retained overall control of its network, including the ability to instruct ONL to create or remove accounts. Neither had put in place sufficiently clear and effective measures to ensure that old accounts were routinely identified and removed." ®

articles.headline: Adam Silver sees the positives of having parity in the NBA with 8 champions in 8 seasons
keyFacts: NBA Commissioner Adam Silver discussed the league's parity and the positives of having eight different champions in eight seasons during an appearance on Good Morning America.
Silver stated that this parity highlights a high level of competition and gives many teams a chance to win championships regardless of market size.
Silver also noted that a global pool of talent allows fans to watch any game on any night with the expectation of seeing compelling basketball.
body: Ever since the Golden State Warriors repeated as champions in 2017 and 2018, no team has won two titles in a row. In fact, there have been eight different champions since the 2018 Finals, with the most recent champion being the New York Knicks, who won their first title in 52 seasons.

Leading up to the 2026-27 NBA season's opening day, League Commissioner Adam Silver went on Good Morning America to talk about the upcoming season. He spoke about the parity with all the teams winning championships, and the positives that stem from it.
NBA Commissioner Adam Silver speaks on why parity is meaningful for the league

Back when the Warriors repeated back in 2017 and 2018, the NBA was extremely different from what it is today. There were plenty of teams that were trying to be competitive, but they just couldn't beat the dominant teams, which were the Warriors and the Cleveland Cavaliers at the time.

Before them were the Miami Heat, the San Antonio Spurs, and the Los Angeles Lakers. All those teams won multiple championships during their heyday, and the Heat and the Lakers even had repeats. That has not happened over the past decade, which just goes to show the quality of teams around the NBA.

While some people might see this as a negative, Silver does not see that perspective at all. He loves what he is seeing from the league's parity, which is a big deal for the NBA and the chances of teams winning championships even if they're not from the biggest of markets.

"It says so much about the level of competition and the parity in this league. It's why I think this is one of the most anticipated seasons because there are so many teams that believe they have a shot this year. When you add that global pool of talent, for people who just love basketball, you can watch any game in any night; there's always something to see," Silver said on Good Morning America about the league's level of competition.

It is hard to argue against Silver's point, but there will be people who will talk about how a certain team dominating would be good for narratives. There will come a time when a team repeats as champions, but at the moment, the parity era in the NBA has led to the sport shining even more due to the quality of basketball around the league.

articles.headline: Masahiro Sakurai Says Gaming Needs Originality Or It ‘Will Die Slowly’
keyFacts: Masahiro Sakurai has ended his Game Designers Award after 16 years, reflecting on the declining importance of originality in the gaming industry.
Sakurai stated that originality has a low impact on sales because players gravitate toward familiar things, warning that the industry will die slowly without new ideas.
Sakurai noted that the rise of AI-generated games copying existing concepts makes original ideas harder to achieve and convey, though he hopes pioneers will help the industry persevere.
body: For the last 16 years at Tokyo Game Show, Masahiro Sakurai has handed out awards centered on game design to celebrate games that do things differently. This year, however, was the final year for this event, and in a new interview, he shared a somewhat bleak reflection on the importance of originality as he discontinued the prize.

Sakuraiâs Game Designers Award was centered on promoting original game design ideas, regardless of sales performance. Winners of the award, not necessarily limited to a single game each year, have included the original Life Is Strange,Â Mario Kart: Home Circuit, Viewfinder, and Scribblenauts. However, during his speech at the awards show last month, he painted a somber picture, lamenting, âThough it may sound rather grave, originality doesnât actually have a strong impact on sales. I think it actually ranks low on the list of priorities for many.â

He compared the problem to the way the novelty of a limited-time drink flavor might fade after it’s been released, although he hopes the games industry hosts enough creative minds to avoid this problem. âThere likely arenât many people who try every single new drink that comes out at convenience stores as soon as itâs released. The more you become accustomed to something, the more you gravitate toward the familiar. Most people tend to only want a taste that matches their preference and is exactly what they expect. But an industry that loses that sort of originality will only die slowly. The industry exists today because there have always been new ideas and experiences, and people making them.â

Reflecting further on the comments in an interview with Denfaminico Gamer, he brings up the design philosophy he brought to creating Kirby and Super Smash Bros. In both cases, their respective genresâ2D platformers and fighting gamesâalready existed, but by focusing on new ways to let players act and interact in these genres, the games stand on their own. Yet coming up with original ideas and conveying this to an audience today is more difficult than ever, he admits.

âThe first important thing is whether or not you can come up with an original idea,â explains Sakurai. âYou might be able to expand on the concept of improving upon an existing idea, but when it comes to creating systems without an easy comparison point, who comes up with that idea? Then, you have to get staff to understand that idea, and itâs difficult to convey that ‘this is why it is fun, because you can do this.’ If youâre a game publisher, itâs difficult to then share that big picture. What are the gameâs selling points?”

He continues, âNowadays, so many games are described as XX-like, or games that resemble another one. In other words, the thing everyone else already wants. But originality means you have to create something that isnât already what people are after, and be deliberate with that. Itâs a high hurdle.â

Something AI only exacerbates, he says. When he first opened the award in 2010, there were only roughly 275 games sold on Steam in a given year, a number now at over 19,000. There are over 8000 titles in this monthâs Steam Next Fest alone, many vibecoded with AI and reliant on copying existent ideas.

According to Sakurai, this only makes original ideas more important. âAlthough 19,000 titles is a lot, I think that number will only grow from now on, because AI will be used to turn them out. Most of them will end up unplayable, and there will be so many that itâll be impossible to keep track or even understand them. With those AI games, the vast majority will be direct copies of games weâve seen before. Thereâs already many of them, even now.

âA little while ago, there was a game called Librarian. Itâs a game set in a magical world, where all the books have been jumbled up and you have to put them back. Thatâs the premise, but the mechanics are simple. So, unsurprisingly, a lot of imitators soon followed. Games like Supermarket Chaos or Needle in a Haystack Simulator have multiplied like crazy. Theyâre all puzzle games, but that kind of imitation will be simple for AI to conduct. But even if AI can create all these sorts of works, such as by analyzing the atmosphere of games from Fumito Ueda like ICO and Shadow of the Colossus and using that to create something similar, which could happen, but AI would not be able to create whatever Ueda himself will create in the future.â

In other words, though Sakurai fears for the future of game originality, if pioneers of game design continue to find the space to create original ideas, then the game industry will persevere. Even if he will no longer present the award he founded, his hope is that originality will find space to thrive. Simply because, without it, there may not be an industry left.

articles.headline: Think social media protects your data? Platforms have racked up $26 billion in privacy penalties since 2020
keyFacts: Global social media platforms accumulated over $26 billion in privacy-related fines and settlements since 2020 according to a Surfshark study.
Meta platforms accounted for $23.7 billion or 91 percent of the total penalties according to the study.
The United States led enforcement with $20.9 billion in fines while European regulators imposed $5.16 billion.
body: - Social platforms have incurred over $26 billion in privacy fines and settlements globally since 2020.
- Meta platforms (Facebook and Instagram) accounted for $23.7 billion (91%) of all penalties.
- The US led enforcement with $20.9 billion in fines, followed by European regulators at $5.16 billion.

Social media platforms thrive on personal data, but failing to protect it is proving exceptionally costly. Since 2020, the world’s top 10 social networks have accumulated more than $26 billion in privacy-related fines and regulatory settlements worldwide.
According to a study published by cybersecurity firm Surfshark, the lion's share of this astronomical financial penalty belongs to one parent company: Meta.
Between Facebook and Instagram, Mark Zuckerberg’s tech empire is responsible for an overwhelming 91% of the worldwide total, racking up $23.7 billion in penalties.
Meta dominates the penalty board
Facebook alone accumulated $14.3 billion in penalties, while Instagram accounted for $9.4 billion. TikTok placed a distant third, tallying $1.6 billion in fines across global jurisdictions.

Other familiar platforms also faced notable regulatory actions. LinkedIn accrued $360 million, YouTube followed with $222 million, and X (formerly Twitter) totaled $151 million. Further down the list, Snapchat recorded $35 million in fines, Reddit registered $19 million, and Discord logged $928,000. Pinterest stood out as the sole platform in the study with zero qualifying privacy penalties.

The United States spearheaded the financial enforcement, imposing $20.9 billion, roughly 80% of all global fines examined. The single largest penalty came from a massive $17.1 billion US settlement involving Facebook and Instagram over allegations that inadequate safeguards exposed minors to deliberately addictive product features.

American authorities also levied $3.69 billion strictly for data-processing offenses, led by Facebook ($2.9 billion), TikTok ($593 million), and X ($150 million). TikTok additionally received an independent $100 million penalty in 2026 over inadequate security safeguards.
European regulators target cross-border transfers and GDPR
Across the Atlantic, European authorities have imposed $5.16 billion in fines under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and national frameworks.

Ireland served as the focal point of enforcement, issuing $4.87 billion, or 94% of Europe’s total, largely because many tech giants maintain their regional headquarters in Dublin. France trailed at $245 million, followed by the UK at $36 million.
Europe’s two heaviest individual fines stemmed from unauthorized international data transfers:
Facebook received a $1.39 billion fine for transferring EU user data to US servers.
TikTok was hit with a $615 million fine for transferring European user data to China, echoing wider scrutiny surrounding apps with ties to foreign jurisdictions.

European regulators also penalized platforms $1.22 billion for unlawful data processing, $1.09 billion for data breach incidents, and $594 million for insufficient technical security safeguards. Regulatory bodies in South Korea and Australia added further pressure, issuing $62.4 million and roughly $50.5 million in fines, respectively.

As lawmakers worldwide tighten regulations, whether battling data misuse or debating proposals that weaken encryption, these multi-billion-dollar sums send an unmistakable message: user privacy can no longer be treated as an afterthought.

articles.headline: Zelenskyy says if Trump can't stop Putin, help Ukraine do it
keyFacts: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that if President Trump cannot stop Russian President Vladimir Putin, the U.S. should provide Ukraine with interceptor missiles.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that President Trump has not deliberately denied weapons to Ukraine and described interceptors as high-demand products globally.
Zelenskyy prepared to meet U.S. envoys in Norway to discuss diplomatic efforts, amid heightened tensions between Kyiv and Washington over weapon shipments and satellite data.
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview published Tuesday that if President Trump "cannot rein Putin in," he should provide long-requested interceptor missiles so Ukraine can defend itself, as the war of words between the two leaders continues to escalate.

"If you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure," Zelenskyy told the Italian newspaper Corriere Della Sera, referring to Russia's autocratic President Vladimir Putin.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said later Tuesday that Mr. Trump has been "frustrated" by what he described as false accusations that "he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine." He insisted that nothing had been "deliberately denied to Ukraine," but added: "It's simply, it's a balance between our obligations to other partners and frankly our own ... requirements for our own facilities as well."
The exchange came as Zelenskyy prepared to meet U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway on Tuesday, with his fellow envoy, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, expected to join remotely.

Zelenskyy has accused the Trump administration this week of delaying shipments of interceptor missiles to Ukraine, as well as constraining Starlink satellite data that is vital to Ukrainian forces' ability to intercept incoming Russian attack drones.

Ukraine has nearly run out of the U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors used to take down Russian ballistic missiles, and Zelenskyy has long pleaded for more. This week he said the U.S. was delaying delivery of Patriots already purchased by European nations for Ukraine.
Rubio, on a visit to India, said "every other country in the world" also wanted Patriots.

"I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," he said. "It's probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field. So, when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying."

The meeting comes as daily Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities , and as relations between Kyiv and Washington appear more strained than they have been since in the Oval Office.

The Ukrainian president said Monday that his country had suffered another night of Russian strikes, "and again there was no warning from partners." At least four people were killed in the capital in the latest attacks, Kyiv officials said Tuesday.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said Finnish President Alexander Stubb would also join the talks in Oslo, with "the aim to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path," according to a statement from the prime minister's office.
Starshield and Patriots
Mr. Trump on Friday , reducing penalties for its energy sales in a bid to ease rising U.S. gas prices caused by the ongoing — a policy Zelenskyy says could embolden Moscow to step up its .
Mr. Trump has criticized Zelenskyy for saying he would resume strikes on Russian refineries in retaliation for the latest Russian onslaught.
Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine was still unable to use Starshield — the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite network — to intercept Russian drones.

The Trump administration has denied ordering Starshield restrictions. A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday that there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."

In recent days, Mr. Trump has intensified his public criticism of Zelenskyy, saying in a Truth Social post that the Ukrainian leader "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," and telling reporters, "maybe it's time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate."

Mr. Trump has never publicly acknowledged that Russia started the war against its neighbor, which initially began in 2014, and has at times for the full-scale invasion ordered by Putin on Feb. 24, 2022.

Ahead of his Tuesday meeting with Mr. Trump's envoys, Zelenskyy said he had a "substantive conversation" with Rubio the previous day in which he stressed that Starshield "needs to be restored" and ballistic missile interceptors "are needed to protect lives."

Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers via video call on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" already paid for by European countries. He said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth hadn't signed off on the shipment.

Multiple European countries were waiting for U.S. approval to transfer their own Patriot interceptors, he added, saying he believed "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."

Rubio said Tuesday that it could be accurate that a batch of interceptors purchased for Ukraine had not been delivered, but he told reporters: "I think the important takeaway for you is that there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine."

Rubio also said Mr. Trump was "frustrated because, first of all, he doesn't like to be blamed for things that aren't true, including accusations that somehow he had ordered intelligence sharing to be cut off. And that's not true. He's said that repeatedly."
"I think the president, more than anything, is responding to the insinuation that somehow he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine — which is not fair and not true," he added.
In his interview with the Italian newspaper, published hours earlier, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had built its relationship with Washington "on honesty, fairness, and, most importantly, transparency."

"When you lie while your people are at war, it is very painful. That is why I have always wanted to hide nothing and never lie to the President of the United States," Zelenskyy told the paper, adding: "We would like to continue having the same open, honest, and pragmatic relations with America that we have today."

"The Russians are striking. America cannot stop them," he said. "Let's believe that America really wants to, but cannot. Then, as a partner, I am willing to meet President Trump halfway: if they strike us and we cannot strike back — that is neither honest nor fair — but if this is what you need, if you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure."
Trump-Xi-Putin summit on Ukraine?
U.S.-led efforts to end the nearly five-year conflict have stalled in recent months, with Washington more focused on its war with Iran.
Mr. Trump recently said he was ready to meet with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next month for talks that could include discussion of the Ukraine war.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has confirmed that "the topic of such a hypothetical has indeed been mentioned."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this week that any such meeting on his country's fate, without Ukraine at the table, would "only encourage Putin to continue this war."

articles.headline: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son says
keyFacts: Dan Mackenzie said his younger siblings were forcibly starved at their grandmother's house until police rescued them two weeks ago.
Paul Mackenzie and 28 other cult leaders were convicted on Monday of murdering 191 people who starved to death.
The cult leader is due to be sentenced on November 6 and still faces separate cases involving terrorism and radicalisation.
body: - Published
The eldest son of Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, convicted of murdering 191 people, says his younger siblings were still being forced to fast as recently as two weeks ago.
Dan Mackenzie, 27, said he reported the case to police, who rescued eight children, including his five younger siblings from their grandmother's house, and took them to a rescue centre.
"They were basically forcibly fasted because they were denying food to them for almost three days," he tells BBC's Newsday.
His father was found guilty on Monday of murdering 190 children and one adult who starved to death in Shakahola forest, near the Kenyan coast.
He had ordered members of his doomsday cult to starve themselves and their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".
Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder.

Dan Mackenzie, who had initially defended his father, said at first he had struggled to understand the allegations against the cult leader, but came to realise the scale of the tragedy during the court proceedings.
"When I was 12, I was forced to fast for almost a week," he says. He also remembers church members beating him for hours to make him attend a service as a child.
Now, he says he felt he had to report family members who still believe in the teachings in order to free his siblings. "I had to report my grandmother."
The cult leader's doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".
"I left school when I was seven," says Dan.
Now living in the coastal town of Malindi, Dan earns a living as a motorcycle taxi driver, supporting himself and his younger siblings.
He said some people in the town had been angry with him because of his father's crimes, but others "had accepted him because he had distanced himself from that life".
"I hope the verdict would bring some comfort to those who had lost friends and relatives," Dan tells BBC's Newsday.
On Monday, Stephen Mwiti, 48, who said he had lost all six of his children to the cult, welcomed the verdict.
"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court.
His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.
Delivering her eight-hour judgment in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".
One of his co-accused told the court that Mackenzie had said anyone who resisted fasting must be forced to go to heaven "through kicks and blows".
Burials in the forest where the cult was based were described as "weddings", with those who died celebrated as having "wedded with Jesus", the judge said.
Mackenzie and other cult leaders also face separate cases involving terrorism, radicalisation and denying children an education.

The murder verdict is the first ruling on the most serious charges against the pastor, who was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were discovered in shallow graves in Shakahola forest, near Kenya's coast.
He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.

The GMKTec K8 Plus is more expensive than it used to be, but still manages to undercut a lot of the so-called 'entry-level' PC market in 2026. With regular discounts, a sturdy handling of lighter and more moderate games, and a unique potential for upgrades from both onboard components and additional eGPUs, it's looking pretty good right now. Mini PCs haven't been shielded from this year's price increases, but the GMKTec K8 Plus still manages to pose a serious threat to Valve's $1,000+ Steam Machine. The AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS box launched a good few years ago, but has nevertheless risen to fame among those looking for a lightweight gaming experience. Its sturdy 1080p performance across some of the most demanding games on the market keeps it fiercely competitive with both cheaper alternatives and more expensive mainstream devices, even if the days of a $500 price tag are long behind us.

The K8 Plus used to be a steady $400 - $500 device, but the 32GB RAM version I've been testing is now more likely to be found between $750 and $900. If you spot it on a good day, though, it could be one of the few last bastions of entry-level PC gaming - assuming you're happy rolling the dice on its WiFi card.

With the best gaming PCs running you thousands of dollars and the best gaming laptops seeing their own inflations, many are looking to integrated GPUs to see them through these troubling years. The GMKTec K8 Plus does much more than its Radeon 780M would suggest, though. With easy upgradeability, a rare Oculink port for additional eGPU access, and a cooling system equipped to deal with gaming's larger challenges, the K8 Plus could give the Steam Machine something serious to think about.

This far into the GMKTec K8 Plus's lifespan, there are only two configurations that sit with consistency on the shelves. Both use the AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS, an octa-core processor with 16 threads and a 54W TDP, partnered with the brand's Radeon 780M integrated graphics. However, the 16GB DDR5 5600MHz RAM model is often available for a couple hundred bucks less than the 32GB version I've been testing.

As it stands, the model sat on my test bench will run you somewhere between $750 and $950 depending on sales (note Amazon's listings generally drop you down to 512GB of storage), whereas the cheaper alternative can drop things down to around $600.
Swipe to scroll horizontally
Design

The GMKTec K8 Plus keeps the same compact form factor you'd expect from a mini PC, with a 58mm height and a pretty square 127 x 132 mm depth and width. It's small enough to sit neatly under a monitor or to one side, though its port placements might get in the way of such a neat setup.

I was initially nervous about the transparent plastic top floating just over the top edge of the main chassis. The twist-off cap provides easy access to four top screws for entry into the main compartment, housing the system's main fan right up top. You'll either love it or hate it.
GamesRadar+'s weekly hardware digest
Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

I can see how those going for a cleaner, more professional look might balk at the plastic hat, but the convenience it brings to the table is undeniable. Plus, anyone bored of the homogeneous box aesthetic will be glad of the more unique design choice here.

Twisting the lid counter-clockwise provides a satisfying snap as it lifts away from the main body of the device, and replacing it is as simple as lining everything up and twisting in the opposite direction.

Everything around that lid also feels solid. A metal casing keeps things looking premium on the desk and in the hands, while that bold green power button provides a little relief from the all-black design. My only concern is the printed 'GMKTec' logo positioned diagonally across the top right edge, which cheapens the aesthetic a little.
Features
The GMKTec K8 Plus has three main weapons in its arsenal: its ability to host a whole bunch of external displays, its Oculink port, and its upgradeability.

Ports aren't plentiful here though; you'll find similarly-sized options with more USB-As on offer around the back. You're still getting two USB-A 2.0 connections for more permanent accessories as well as two USB 3.2s at the front for easier access as well. On paper, those dual USB 4 slots are holding their own as well, and we haven't even mentioned the twin RJ45 Ethernet slots.

Tallying those connections with the HDMI 2.1 and DisplayPort, you've got space for up to four external displays to run here - perfect for those building a more substantial workstation from a smaller device.

That's not all, though. The front of the device also plays host to an Oculink connection, a rarity even across mini PCs designed more specifically around gaming. It allows you to (probably later down the line, looking at current GPU prices) attach an external GPU for a boost in performance should you require it. It's also a boon for those building a home NAS server, allowing for additional SATA connections.

Port placement could present some concerns here. The USB 4 required for that final fourth external display is positioned around the front, next to the Oculink. It's a small gripe, but that's going to make for a slightly messier setup when everything's firing on all cylinders. I would have loved to see at least the Oculink's more permanent connection situated out of sight towards the back.

Finally, that aforementioned twist-off lid provides easy access to RAM and storage upgrades. Once you've got those four screws holding the fan down away you're in to swap out for up to 96GB of SODIMM memory and up to 4TB of M.2 2280 storage.
Performance

The GMKTec K8 Plus can hold its own in lighter games, speeding through Restory, Stardew Valley, and Islanders with only a little stutter here and there. It's a perfectly playable experience for these less demanding games, often at a lower price than you'd find elsewhere on the market.

Putting the K8 Plus to the test against something a little meatier shows its limits, though. It still holds its own in full Triple-A releases, as long as they're a little older, slimmer, or offer additional optimization tools.

Shadow of the Tomb Raider, Total War: Three Kingdoms, and Cyberpunk 2077 hold their own in the 40-fps range when under Medium settings here. That's not the super smooth 60fps many aim for, but it's running - and with prices the way they are, I'll certainly take it.
Yes, things fall off a cliff slightly when we get to High graphical settings - though Tomb Raider manages to hold its own here much better than the heavier titles in my benchmarking roster.

Suffice to say, the GMKTec K8 Plus will run a sturdy Steam library, but you'll need to be taking advantage of additional FSR tools baked into that Radeon 780M GPU to reach the kinds of speeds you'll find in more expensive machines. If you just play lighter indie titles, though, you're pretty set.

The GMKTec K8 Plus doesn't just want to play your games, though. This is a compact mini PC designed to power through day-to-day productivity as well. AMD's components scored 2,218 in their single core Geekbench 7 benchmark here, with 13,410 in multi-core performance. Considering the size and price point, that's certainly a result in GMKTec's favor.

Unfortunately, there's one glaring issue I ran into almost every day when running the GMKTec K8 Plus. This thing's WiFi card is fried. While it can hold its own in day-to-day web browsing, downloads represent a particular challenge for the out-the-box connectivity, often requiring me to leave it running overnight for a job that would take most other machines an hour or so. The K8 Plus allows for WiFi card upgrades, and it's not an expensive part to replace, but I'd factor the cost into this rig's price tag before checkout.
Should you buy the GMKTec K8 Plus?

If you're willing to roll the dice on those internet speeds, or swap out your WiFi card straight from the off, the GMKTec K8 Plus actually represents solid value in today's market. It's going to hold its own against the Steam Machine in day-to-day 1080p performance, while coming in remarkably cheaper (especially on its best days). You'll also enjoy the benefits of a full Windows productivity suite for your cash, as well as that easy-access upgradeability - not to mention the flexibility of that Oculink port later down the line.
How I tested the GMKTec K8 Plus

I've had the GMKTec K8 Plus on my desk for two weeks, running the mini PC for all my work and most of my play during that time. Aside from a few Doom: The Dark Ages and Planet Coaster 2 skirmishes, this hub has been my destination for lighter gaming across Stardew Valley, Islanders, and Restory, with in-game benchmarks tested at both high and medium graphical settings in Shadow of the Tomb Raider, Total War: Three Kingdoms, Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered, and Cyberpunk 2077. The CPU was also tested using Geekbench 7. Each of these benchmarks was performed three times, with the final result representing an average of all runs.

articles.headline: SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation
keyFacts: Reliable Robotics raised $115 million in a Series D funding extension, pushing the startup's valuation beyond $1 billion.
CEO Robert Rose said the funds will support efforts to get the company's autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration.
Rose expects the startup to receive its first system certification in 18 to 24 months.
body: Reliable Robotics has been working for nearly a decade to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft. Now, with a $115 million funding boost, the Mountain View, California-based startup has a longer runway as it pushes to get its autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration — a critical milestone that co-founder and CEO Robert Rose said the startup is inching toward.

The financing is an extension of its Series D round and includes $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round, which now totals $275 million, has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark. Other investors include Gideon Strategic Partners, RockCreek, Geek Ventures, Gold Hill Capital, Sparkwave Capital and others. Reliable has raised $380 million to date.

“We continue to make steady progress and deliver evidence to the FAA and every day, we inch closer and closer,” said Rose, a former director of flight software at SpaceX who has also had stints at Tesla and Google. Reliable co-founder and CTO Juerg Frefel is also a SpaceX veteran who spent nearly a decade there as an engineer.
And in aviation — one of the most regulated industries in the world — moving toward certification of new technology is progress.
Reliable Robotics is working to gain FAA certification on four fronts, all of which are linked to its goal of autonomous flight.

Its first product, called continuous autopilot engagement, handles the engine startup, taxiing, takeoff, and landing for the pilot, who remains in the aircraft and interacts with the autonomous flight system through a touchscreen. Rose expects to receive certification for this critical first system in 18 to 24 months.
The second certification, which Rose says is at least three years away, removes the pilot from the cockpit and moves them to a ground-control station.

Reliable is also working toward certification of a collision-avoidance radar, which the company has developed in-house after failing to attract legacy suppliers to take on the project. Most conventional radar systems use an antenna that moves to scan the surrounding airspace. Reliable has developed a solid-state radar that has no moving parts and scans the sky at a longer range and at much higher resolution, according to Rose. It’s also easier to maintain because there are no moving parts and it costs less, he added.

“This is of great interest to operators these days, given the collisions that we’ve had recently in commercial aviation,” he said, adding that the radar also works on the ground to prevent collisions with other aircraft or infrastructure. Rose expects the solid-state radar to be certified by the end of 2027.

The final certification is for its airline, called Reliable Airlines, which will be the first airline certified to use the autonomous flying technology. The airline is based in Albuquerque and uses six Cessna Caravans — workhorses of the aviation industry — to fly cargo six days a week. (The FAA certifies equipment, but the agency also must certify the airline operations under a separate set of regulations.)
While the certification process is lengthy, Nimble Partners founder John Burbank said the benefits will be broad and significant.

“It’s a much bigger effort and much bigger opportunity than to just build one plane,” Burbank said, noting that Reliable is building a system that can be adopted by any airframe. “They had a really big vision nine years ago, and saw this as something needed and essential. Once they get the first one approved, then everyone will realize this is going to be the path for the industry, just as we’re seeing the path for the auto industry being autonomous.”

articles.headline: How to stop fake virus pop-ups on your Windows PC
keyFacts: Fake virus pop-ups on Windows PCs are scareware scams designed to induce panic, steal money, or install malware.
Users can encounter these deceptive alerts through browser pop-ups or unauthorized website notifications enabled via deceptive permission prompts.
People can remove these malicious pop-ups by terminating the browser tab, force-quitting the browser, clearing site data, or removing unauthorized extensions and apps.
body: How to stop fake virus pop-ups on your Windows PC
That "critical Microsoft alert" is a scam that tricks you into installing actual malware.

You're browsing as normal, when all of a sudden you see an urgent pop-up flashing an alarming warning that your computer has been infected with a virus. The good news is these alerts are almost always fake: they sometimes occur when websites have been compromised and send notifications to make you think your computer is infected. But if you fall for this, you may actually download malware.

Cybersecurity researchers call these tactics "scareware," because they induce a state of panic for those on the receiving end. They're not uncommon: one strain of browser-based scareware called CypherLoc has hit more than 2.8 million people since the start of 2026, according to a study from security firm Barracuda.

Like many attacks, the goal here is gaining access to your computer or stealing your money. They will usually direct you to call a bogus tech support phone number, convince you to download an anti-malware scanner that's itself malicious or have you hand over payment information. Some malicious pop-ups can even be cloaked as security features; one scam flagged by the FTC involves using fake CAPTCHA requests to install malware on devices.
While these screens are scary, they are thankfully not difficult to thwart once you know where they're coming from and how to close them.
Why do I keep getting notifications that I have a virus?

Pop-ups involved in these scams create urgency with dramatic wording like "Critical Threat Detected!" and often use flashing lights, bright colors and even alarm sounds to increase the "scare" factor. You might hear a robotic voice announcing a "critical Microsoft security alert," or the site could even show you your IP address.

Sometimes these scams use the names of legitimate security companies to increase the likelihood that you'll fall for them, sporting titles like McAfee Security Software or Windows Defender. But why are you getting them?

Fake virus attacks can either be delivered through browser pop-ups or your computer's notification center. Both methods typically result from opening an unsafe link or visiting a malicious website, though rogue ads can sneak through even on legitimate pages. Cybercriminals abuse advertising spaces so when you click a compromised banner, it redirects you to a fake security warning page. The pop-ups are forced into full-screen mode, often with your mouse cursor hidden, to make you think you're stuck.

Alternatively, you might see smaller alerts in the corner of your screen if you've inadvertently granted a website permission to send notifications. When you visit a new site that wants to send notifications — even a legitimate one — you'll be asked to click Allow to provide this permission in your browser. This is often given under false pretense, with the website saying something like "Click Allow to read more." The site then gains permission to send push notifications directly through Windows' notification center, making the alerts look like official warnings. And sites you've approved can send notifications even if you don't have them open.
How can I get rid of scareware pop-ups?

If you get a full-screen pop-up saying you have a virus, do not click anything on the page. These pop-ups often hijack the browser and make it difficult to close without clicking on unsafe links. If possible, the most efficient response is to terminate the offending tab using your browser's built-in task manager; the shortcut is Shift + Escape for Chrome, Edge and Firefox. Look for a tab with an outlandish label like "Security Alert!" and close it using End Task or the X button to the right of the process. F11 is the shortcut to get the browser out of full-screen mode.

If that doesn't work, you'll need to force-quit your browser entirely. Open the Task Manager by pressing Ctrl + Shift + Esc, then click the Processes tab on the left. Should that fail, hit Ctrl + Alt + Del and open the Task Manager from that menu. Click Name to sort with active apps at the top, then right-click your browser and choose End task. If you have the option enabled to start from your last session when reopening your browser, don't accept the option to reopen closed tabs since that will load the scam page again.

In case the notifications persist, delete recent cookies and other site data from your browser (Ctrl + Shift + Del on Chrome and Edge). You should also go through the list of sites that are allowed to send notifications to check for any you don't recognize. In Chrome, click the three vertical dots at the top-right of the browser, choose Settings, then go to Privacy and security > Site settings > Notifications. In the Allowed to send notifications section, click the three-dot menu on the right for any unknown websites and choose Remove or Block. To silence all pings, pick Don't allow sites to send notifications at the top.

Browser extensions can also be the source of these schemes. Click the puzzle piece icon at the top-right of your browser and then choose Manage extensions to see a list of everything you have installed. Remove any unknown items or those you haven't used in a while. Restart your browser when done to ensure your changes take effect.

Further pop-ups could be caused by junk apps installed on your computer. Press Win + I to open Settings, then navigate to Apps > Installed apps. Go through the list and uninstall anything that looks shady.
How to avoid actual malware in the future

Ironically, when your computer is actually infected, it typically doesn't come with flashing warnings. Regular computer scans are the key to detecting subtle malware that could be silently running on your device. Windows offers built-in protection with Microsoft Defender, which is good enough for most people. You can download additional software for a second opinion; Malwarebytes, which is free and features an on-demand scanner, is a good backup option.

Malwarebytes also offers a browser extension called Browser Guard, which can add another layer of protection against malicious pop-ups in your browser. This service also stops general trackers and obnoxious advertising. These measures, coupled with your computer's built-in protection, should be sufficient for keeping yourself safe online.

articles.headline: Helldivers 2 swaps over to Easy anti-cheat, with developers admitting Gameguard "wasn't as effective as it could have been"
keyFacts: Arrowhead Game Studios announced that Helldivers 2 is replacing its GameGuard anti-cheat system with Easy Anti-Cheat.
Developers stated the switch aims to better protect fair gameplay and the integrity of the game.
Arrowhead confirmed that the shift means some non-malicious cosmetic mods will need to be updated to function.
body: Helldivers will be switching up its anti-cheat, as developer Arrowhead Game Studios has admitted that its Gameguard cheat policy "wasn't as effective as it could have been."

In a post made to the game's Steam page (not available in the UK - get that VPN on), the team explains the decision: "The implementation of GameGuard for Helldivers 2 wasn't as effective as it could have been [...] In the end we decided to take another path with EAC. EAC is an industry standard used in over 200 games, and we believe this will be an effective way to protect the Galactic War and will better protect fair gameplay and the integrity of the game."

As part of this shift, Arrowhead also confirmed that several non-malicious mods, such as cosmetic changes, will need to be updated to work alongside Easy Anti-Cheat. "We know mods are part of the DNA of PC gaming and gaming communities as a whole. In general, we appreciate the creativity behind cosmetic and non-gameplay mods, which players can enjoy without negatively impacting those who play alongside them," the post reads.

"Where we need to improve is how we protect players against modifications that create unfair advantages or negatively impact others, which goes beyond software manipulation to tamper with our game. These changes mean that some mods, particularly the types that are affecting the experience of other players, may no longer function."

The post continues to implore those who feel a non-malicious mod has been blocked by Easy Anti-Cheat to reach out via Zendesk. So, there should be a bit of a rough transitional period, but hopefully a lot of the fun mods should be good to go again in the near future.

It's indeed true that Easy Anti-Cheat has become the norm for a vast variety of PC games. However, regardless of the anti cheat being used, those in the UK are still unable to play Helldivers 2 due to a mysterious issue. Sony has promised to address the issue with Valve, but as of writing there's been no resolution to the problem.

articles.headline: Trump continues midterm campaign blitz in North Carolina – US politics live

Whatley trails Democrat Roy Cooper in polls, while a Republican super PAC pulled 71 million dollars in North Carolina ad spending.

body: Trump continues midterm campaign blitz in North Carolina – US politics live
President to stump for Michael Whatley, who is facing an uphill battle against Democrat Roy Cooper for the Senate, as elections are just two weeks away
Trump continues midterm campaign blitz in North Carolina
Welcome to the US politics live blog! I’m Shrai Popat and I’ll be bringing you the latest lines from Washington and beyond.

We start today with Donald Trump’s upcoming to trip to Greenville, North Carolina – where he’ll stump for Michael Whatley, the Republican nominee for US Senate, facing an uphill battle against Roy Cooper, the state’s former Democratic governor who has consistently led Whatley in the polls for the open seat.

North Carolina is the president’s second stop in a seven-day campaign blitz across a number of states that he won in 2024. It’s all to drum up support for Republican candidates on the ballot ahead of the midterms – now just two weeks away.

However, earlier this month, the Senate’s top GOP Super Pac announced it pulled a $71m ad spend in North Carolina, in order to funnel more money into the Kansas race – a sign that Republicans’ hopes to hold on to the Tar Heel state might be dwindling.
On Monday, Trump rallied in Kansas – as the Senate competition there becomes increasingly tight.
A reminder that my colleagues are covering the latest news out of France, following riots that saw thousands arrested over the weekend, and curfews implemented.
Donald Trump has pushed baseless claims that the riots – which began as protests against the country’s crumbling education system – are due to mass migration.

The president repeated the falsehoods, even though French authorities have given no indication that immigrants are responsible for the riots. It didn’t stop Trump from kicking off his Kansas rally by playing a Fox News report ahead of his appearance on stage, which showed looting and destruction after chaos erupted in France.
Trump announces relief for farmers impacted by soaring diesel prices, as Iran war continues and midterms loom
Donald Trump has announced $8bn worth of economic aid for farmers hit by soaring diesel prices, as polling shows Republicans on course for a midterms drubbing.
The president’s announcement came 15 days before a midterm election dominated by anger over rising fuel costs caused by the US war on Iran.
Farmers in Kansas, a heavily agricultural state, have been hit hard by the consequences of the Iran war. A gallon of diesel costs nearly $6, nearly double from this time a year ago.

In August, the president upset cattle ranchers with a plan to reduce import tariffs to lower the price of beef and with aggressive immigration raids that prompted some agricultural workers to stay at home.

Trump’s announcement came during a rally in Kansas on Monday night as Republicans faced mounting anger over the cost of living and the ongoing war in Iran. As my colleague David Smith wrote last night: “The fact that Donald Trump was here at all said more about a looming electoral disaster facing his Republican party next month than anything contained in his dark and discursive 98-minute stump speech.”

Trump seemed to acknowledge there was a risk Democrats could win in the state, where no Democrat has won a US Senate seat since 1932. As he stumped for first-term senator Roger Marshall, the president told the crowd: “You’re really sort of – I hate to say it – you’re sort of tending toward the purple,” the president told about 5,000 supporters in a multipurpose arena outside Wichita, acknowledging that Kansas already has a Democratic governor in Laura Kelly. “That’s why I have to be sure that we get this guy.”

articles.headline: Adobe Lightroom mobile can now open closed eyes in photos with a simple tap
keyFacts: Adobe announced that the mobile version of Lightroom can now open closed eyes in photos using generative AI.
The app displays a new Open Eyes Quick Action icon when it detects closed eyes in an image.
Free users can test the feature twice before requiring a subscription to an Adobe Creative Cloud plan.
body: Adobe announced yesterday that the mobile version of Lightroom, available for iOS, iPadOS, and Android, can now open closed eyes in photos using generative AI with just a single tap. When the app detects a person, or a group of people, have their eyes closed in a photo it will automatically present users with a new Open Eyes Quick Action that appears as an icon over the image providing easy access to the new feature.
Adobe Lightroom mobile can now open closed eyes in photos with a simple tap
When the mobile app detects closed eyes in a photo it will present users with a new Open Eyes Quick Action tool.

Being able to easily save an otherwise great photo by opening a subject’s eyes has been a feature in Adobe’s Photoshop Elements for nearly a decade, but as DPReview points out, Elements sources the replacement from another photo of the subject with mixed results depending on variations between the two images. Open Eyes in Lightroom mobile instead relies on generative AI so the replacement eyes match the lighting and pose, and the app will use other images of the same person in your Lightroom library as reference so the open eyes will accurately match the color, size, and shape of their own.

You can perform a similar fix in other Adobe apps like Photoshop using its own generative AI tools, but it’s not a one-tap fix, and it’s not free. Those using the free version of the Lightroom mobile app can try the Open Eyes feature twice before they’re given a prompt to subscribe to an Adobe Creative Cloud plan that includes more credits for its various AI-powered tools, according to DPReview.
