articles.headline: More than 250,000 displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated: UNHCR
keyFacts: More than 250,000 people were internally displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated in July, according to the UNHCR.
The UNHCR stated that shelter, food, and cash assistance are the most immediate needs for the displaced population.
The United Kingdom announced it would deploy Royal Air Force jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks.
body: More than 250,000 people have been internally displaced in Yemen since the country’s war reignited in July, the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) has said, as fighting between Houthi rebels and forces loyal to the internationally recognised government rages across several fronts.

The city of Taiz in southwestern Yemen is at the centre of the displacement crisis, accounting for 76 percent of departures and hosting 52 percent of those newly displaced, UNHCR said in a statement on Tuesday.
Lahij in southwestern Yemen hosts 23 percent of the newly displaced population, followed by Aden in the south with 13 percent, UNHCR said.

“Shelling intensified in Taiz, including in residential areas and around health facilities, while insecurity and restrictions along key routes continue to constrain humanitarian access and movement,” the agency said in a statement.

The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, the interim capital of the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government.

“The most immediate needs that we’ve been able to identify are around shelter, food, and multi-purpose cash assistance,” UNHCR spokesperson Matthew Saltmarsh told a news conference in Geneva, Switzerland.
The agency said about 33,700 families still require shelter assistance amid severe underfunding of the humanitarian response to the war.

Separately, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said in a statement that escalating fighting and fuel shortages in Taiz are threatening its water systems that serve an estimated three million people, including at least 1.6 million children.

“Already one of Yemen’s most water-scarce areas, Taiz is now facing renewed pressure on its most essential services for thousands of displaced families,” said Akhil Iyer, UNICEF’s Yemen representative, at a press briefing in Geneva.
The warnings come as fighting intensifies between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthis.
The death toll from a Houthi ballistic missile strike on a military training camp in Yemen’s Shabwa governorate increased to at least 58, local authorities said.

The Yemeni government described the site as a security training centre away from the front lines, while Houthi forces said they targeted Saudi-backed forces. Hospitals faced blood shortages in Ataq as medical teams responded to casualties and families searched for missing relatives.
The attack was followed by retaliatory strikes by government forces near Taiz, raising further concerns over the worsening humanitarian crisis in Yemen.

Reporting from the capital, Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said, “The Houthis are not backing down. Their military spokesman says they are continuing to conduct more missile attacks deep inside Saudi Arabia.”
“As cross-border attacks grow, Yemenis fear the war is coming closer to home, especially as both sides threaten to escalate their attacks, while Saudi Arabia steps up its air campaign,” Mawry added.
Meanwhile, Yemen’s Saudi-backed coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said on Tuesday that its forces have destroyed 127 Houthi weapons depots and missile launch platforms.
Separately, the United Kingdom said it would deploy Royal Air Force jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi Arabia from increasing Houthi attacks.
The British Ministry of Defence said in a statement that the Typhoon warplanes would operate in a “defensive role” and not carry out attacks against the Houthis.

Tensions have soared in Yemen since July, when the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi ports, and fighting escalated sharply last month when they seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the government along the Red Sea coast.

Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded to the losses with a counteroffensive and launched Operation Dawn of Yemen, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including Sanaa, seized by the group in 2014.

articles.headline: Final Fantasy Resonance review – An anniversary celebration worth the ride
keyFacts: Destructoid reviewed Final Fantasy Resonance, a spin-off celebrating the franchise's 40th anniversary with 2D character sprites on 3D backgrounds.
The game features turn-based combat and classic series characters as equipable Visions, though it retains odd gacha-style cinematic attack scenes.
The reviewer stated that while the story and main characters are generic, the game is worth playing for its nostalgia, art style, and side quests.
body: Nostalgia is a hell of a drug, and Final Fantasy Resonance is full of it, in some unique and fun ways.

Largely repurposed from the remnants of the Final Fantasy: Brave Exvius mobile game, Resonance utilizes heroes and villains from the past as gameplay mechanics to assist in battle, and it’s all presented in a beautiful art style featuring 2D character sprites on top of well-made 3D backgrounds.

An open world map, turn-based battles, and cheesy story bring it all together to make a game that’s worth the price of admission if you’re looking for a JRPG reminiscent of a time long gone, especially in the current era of action combat that the franchise is now known for.
A glorious vision

Screenshot by Destructoid For some Final Fantasy fans, “2D” and “turn-based” is all they have to hear to be excited. And with Resonance , it rings true, because playing through its several dozens of hours feels like taking a trip into the past in mostly good ways.

Resonance tells the tale of two knights named Rain and Lasswell, tasked with protecting the Kingdom of Grandshelt. They come into contact with a mysterious woman named Fina and learn of a nefarious plot from a group of armored villains known as the Sworn Six of Paladia, who are out to destroy the world’s important elemental crystals. Yeah, crystals again.

Rain, Lasswell, and Fina head out on an important adventure to save the world from the Sworn Six, and along the way they enlist the help of assist-like characters called Visions, scattered throughout the world map. These Visions are classic characters from each entry in the Final Fantasy series, like Cloud from FF7, Terra from FF8, Noctis from FF15 , Tidus from FF10 , Firion from FF2, and so on.

These Visions can be equipped like a piece of gear, and they stand beside the heroes in battle, offering them their own abilities on top of more that they can acquire as they level up an affinity with them. It’s here that the game is unique from other FF titles, but also where its gacha origins are most felt.

In Brave Exvius, these Visions were part of a gacha mechanic, and they come with odd out-of-place FMV-like scenes that play out when their special attacks are triggered. These really stick out in Resonance , as does a star-tier rank-up system like you’d find in just about any other gacha title, unlocking additional abilities to equip. The only difference now is that it’s all in the game, easy to find, and not tied behind paid RNG.

These particular scenes are very weird to see, like having FF7 Remake’s Cloud Strife pop up in all of his CGI glory, overlaid on top of the game’s normal 2D-3D style, and they really took me out of the moment every time they showed up. They can be skipped, but are no less weird to experience, especially since they just appear to be stock footage with Japanese VO only.

Screenshot by Destructoid Outside of this minor drawback, the turn-based combat is a great return to the series’ origins. This time, it’s centered around exploiting elemental weaknesses and a stagger system that’s used to interrupt your foes’ powerful abilities through different phases of a fight, allowing your team to combine for group attacks and the aforementioned Vision powers to punish foes into submission. It’s reminiscent of Octopath Traveler’s Break system, albeit simpler.
Past meets future

Screenshot by Destructoid Where Resonance fell short for me is its story and world. While it uses crystals and Visions to pull its most iconic heroes from past games, the world that this particular story exists in is rather generic and flat in comparison. Rain and Lasswell are not particularly interesting protagonists, and I felt like it took a good nine or 10 hours for the plot events to really grab me in any way after a long introductory setup period. Couple that with a lot of cringy dialogue and a plain setting, and there’s a lot to be desired from the presentation in Resonance.

I enjoyed several of the game’s additional party members a bit more, like the enigmatic Fina, who is struggling with repressed memories and can somehow command powerful summons, or battle strategist Nichol and his ability to change formations mid-battle to supply different buffs. But I also found the villains to be a bit lacking and cartoonish, making for some serious eye-roll moments throughout.

Where the game does excel a bit more, however, is its side quests. These optional quests offer important exposition, worldbuilding, and gear that you can equip throughout the story, and were arguably my favorite part of the adventure. I’d highly suggest doing them all as they show up, especially since fast travel around the world map makes a bunch of them a breeze to accomplish. It’s through these ancillary characters and normal everyday people that the game’s story felt most meaningful to me.

And of course, it is a Final Fantasy game, so the usual suspects are all also here: Moogles, airships, “Cid,” Cactuars, Gilgamesh, Bahamut, etc. Additionally, along with the Visions, there are classic summons called Espers that you can recruit to your cause. Their special attack cutscenes (animated in 2D) are a true beauty to sit back and watch, adding another wrinkle to how you fight your battles.

But in the end, the game is carried heavily by its art style and nostalgia, which makes it a fitting spin-off for Square Enix to release for the beloved franchise’s 40th anniversary. And if you grew up with the SNES titles, or even came to love the pixel remakes in recent years, then this is definitely worth your time.

Screenshot by Destructoid And honestly? This alone made it feel worth it to me, without taking anything else about the game into account. It just felt nice to play a classic-style Final Fantasy game like this, especially with such a charming aesthetic. But if you’re looking for a gripping narrative and memorable new characters, then you may come away a bit disappointed.
The post Final Fantasy Resonance review – An anniversary celebration worth the ride appeared first on Destructoid .

articles.headline: Fox News Power Rankings: Trump country at a crossroads
keyFacts: Rural support for Republicans has dropped, with under half of rural voters saying they will support the GOP again in November.
Prominent independent candidates are challenging Republicans in four rural Senate races on anti-establishment platforms.
Fox News Power Rankings shifted Florida's gubernatorial race from Likely R to Lean R as Hispanic support for Republicans declined.
body: Republicans have had their share of good and bad election nights this century, but they’ve usually been able to count on the heartland.
Once evenly divided, rural voters have become substantially more Republican over the last two decades. Nearly two-thirds of these voters backed President Trump in the 2024 election.
REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY.
Today, just under half of rural voters say they’ll support the GOP again in November.

Like other groups, rural Americans are concerned about paying the bills. Nineteen percent said the rising cost of living is their biggest economic problem in a recent survey , with gas and energy costs not far behind.
The Trump administration has, in part, tried to counter those anxieties by talking about job growth and the AI boom, but rural voters are frustrated about those issues too.

Less than a quarter of rural voters say the economy is in good shape, and unemployment is a focal point: 8% called a lack of jobs and unemployment their biggest economic issue, and only 28% thought there were good or excellent job opportunities in their communities.
DAVID MARCUS: ON THE GROUND IN MIDDLE AMERICA, FOUR ISSUES WILL DECIDE THE SENATE, AND NONE ARE AFFORDABILITY

Data centers are part of the story too. Only 2% called it their biggest economic problem, but that number is larger than it seems. For 1 in 50 rural voters, data centers are a bigger problem than housing, the cost of living, or getting a job.
These factors have put the Republicans in a tough spot all over the map.

They are a reason why heartland states like Ohio and Iowa have been competitive most of the year and why more rural districts, including some that Trump won by double digits, are becoming margin-of-error races.

Even setting the polls aside, there are signs that the rural vote is on shakier footing. TV viewers in Wyoming will see ads this week for Republican candidate Chuck Gray that don’t mention Trump or the GOP. Two years ago, Trump won 71.6% of the vote there — his best performance in any state, in any election.
Low rural turnout or party switching would make many races closer than the GOP would like, including in Florida, Mississippi and South Carolina.
Four states are worth singling out thanks to another complicating factor.
TRUMP-ALIGNED CONSERVATIVE EMERGES FROM CROWDED PRIMARY TO DECIDE WHO FILLS WYOMING’S LONE HOUSE SEAT
This year, prominent independent candidates are running for Senate against a Republican in four rural-heavy states: Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and South Dakota.
They are pushing anti-establishment policies like congressional term limits and lobbying bans and have a heavy focus on corruption, the top voter concern in last week’s Fox News poll .
And all four say they won’t caucus with either party or would form their own independent caucus if they were elected.

With the Democratic brand still relatively weak around the country and abysmal in these states, the party has stepped out of the race entirely in three of the four (in Montana, a Democrat is staying on the ballot, though support for her has declined).

Normally, frustrated partisans stay home in scenarios like these, leaving the incumbent party to win by a more modest margin. This year, those voters have the ability to turn out for a different candidate, so the margin may get narrower.
FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS THE HOUSE FALLS, THE SENATE STAYS IN PLAY

All these states have been competitive over the last decade or so. Former Sen. Jon Tester, a Democrat, held on to his seat in Montana in 2018; Republicans have scored single-digit victories in South Dakota and Nebraska (where the same independent is running again this year), and even Idaho had a gubernatorial race that came within 15 points back in 2014.
These states could be close again.
In this week’s Power Rankings, two gubernatorial races get more competitive as the final two weeks of campaigning begin.

The Sunshine State is the beating heart of the "MAGA" movement. Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis have posted stronger results each time they’ve run, with the latter winning his last re-election bid by nearly 20 points.
Thanks in part to those performances, Republicans have carved out structural advantages, including a 1.5 million registered voter gap and a resilient get-out-the-vote operation.
But DeSantis’ first win came within around 30,000 votes (or 0.4 points) and in a similar environment to the one we’re in now.

Here, Hispanic voters will play an outsized role, and polls suggest that a large chunk of them have shifted away from the GOP. In last week’s national Fox survey , 31% of Hispanic voters said they preferred the Republican candidate over the Democrat. That’s down 12 points from their support for Trump in 2024.

The Republican candidate, Rep. Byron Donalds, will be pleased to have the endorsement of DeSantis. He remains popular in the state. Donalds still has the edge against Democrat and former Rep. David Jolly, who is hoping former President Bill Clinton can shore up his support when they appear together for the first time today.
Still, this race is no sure thing for the GOP. Florida moves from Likely R to Lean R.

In Nebraska, Republican Gov. Jim Pillen is looking for a second term in office. He cruised to victory the first time with a 23-point win, but with both suburban and rural voters wavering on Trump this cycle, this could be a tougher battle.
Three other factors are playing a role.

First, the presence of Dan Osborn, one of the four notable independents on the ballot in Senate races this year, could boost Democratic turnout for challenger Lynne Walz in a governor’s race that would otherwise attract less attention.
There’s Pillen himself, who has faced some local pushback over a 5% budget cut and hiring freeze within state government.

Finally, the ballot, which will feature third-party challenger Brett Lindstrom, a former state lawmaker who lost to Pillen in a Republican primary four years prior. He’ll appear on the ballot as an "America First" candidate. The party was founded in July.

articles.headline: California’s dysfunction should stay in California
keyFacts: Author Chad Hagan stated that California is experiencing an exodus of businesses, residents, and wealthy individuals due to high taxes and regulations.
According to the article, California Department of Finance data shows a net domestic out-migration of 288,600 people in 2025.
The article asserts that political mismanagement, expensive living costs, and regulatory failures have severely damaged California's economy and quality of life.
body: As the midterm elections approach, liberals are bragging about California as a beacon of progress and economic success.
This is one of my biggest issues with California. As someone who has done business in the state and published a book about it, my question is: What exactly is there to celebrate?

A continuing exodus of businesses and residents? High taxes ? Some of the most expensive housing in the country? Excessive regulatory policies? One of the worst standards of living for the money in America? An enormous and costly welfare system? One of the least competitive business tax climates in the nation? The steady erosion of future economic opportunity? Or perhaps watching so many of the extraordinary achievements of the last century gradually unravel under the weight of political mismanagement?

According to research by the Hoover Institution, more than 350 corporate headquarters departed the Golden State between 2018 and 2021 alone, including nearly a dozen Fortune 1000 companies such as Tesla, Oracle, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise, among others.

And what about the exodus of ultra-high-net-worth individuals and billionaires? While many on California’s political left celebrate their departure, do they not realize the enormous share of the state’s income tax burden shouldered by its wealthiest residents? Beyond taxation, these individuals contribute substantially to a healthy state economy.

In 2021, the number of companies that relocated out of the world’s fifth-largest economy doubled from 2020, earning the state 48th place in the Tax Foundation’s 2022 State Business Tax Climate Index rankings. The state’s 8.84% corporate tax rate is no doubt part of the problem, as is its annual franchise tax for LLCs — the highest in the country — making the costs of running even a small business a burden for any entrepreneur, alongside the unusually high costs of property, labor, permits, and compliance.

For the same reasons, California is witnessing an unprecedented population decline. In fact, many believe, myself included, that California’s peak population days are behind them. California’s Department of Finance estimates that net domestic out-migration was 288,600 people in 2025, meaning that significantly more people left California for other states than arrived from them. This was the largest loss of any state in the country, according to Census data. Presumably, affordability is a driving factor, considering the average cost of living in California is 38% higher than the national average, housing is 97% higher, and California is home to the nation’s highest income tax rates. According to a recent poll, two-thirds of Californians now say their quality of life would be improved if they lived elsewhere.

If liberals truly regard California as an economic model for the rest of the country, how do they explain these inconvenient facts? And if their philosophies take control of Congress in the fall, how will this dysfunction affect other states?

California can’t even dispose of trash correctly. The Chiquita Canyon Landfill was the second-biggest active landfill in the Los Angeles area, but, with some legitimate concerns like an underground chemical reaction that generated noxious odors and massively complex regulations where federal, state, and local requirements overlapped and sometimes contradicted, it ended active waste disposal at the end of 2024.

The same politicians who helped create the noxious regulations that killed the landfill have also created the incentives for illegal dumping and more expensive trash removal. One small business owner was charged an $1,800 trash fee because the trash man had to open a lock. Then there’s the fee thrown on residents last year because — wait for it — Los Angeles liberals realized subsidizing trash removal was too expensive.
Sure, they shut down a smelly landfill with some concerning maintenance challenges. But they also just made the problem worse.

Of course, Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA) will ignore the Los Angeles governance failures, just like he and everyone else ignored the nearby empty reservoir until the 2025 fires were burning bright. Just like he ignored San Francisco’s trash and homelessness problem until China’s communists visited, and just as he pretends the high-speed railroad will ever be built.

For decades, California had a reputation as a world-class business and economic powerhouse. But those days are now long gone. Unfortunately, stifling regulations, an over-bureaucratic governing style, a deteriorating quality of life, and political leadership that treats its assets as permission to excessively tax anyone who calls the state home are driving businesses and residents elsewhere.
DON’T CALIFORNIA AMERICA

States need enforceable environmental standards that protect their residents, but the purpose of that oversight should be to produce solutions at a cost reasonable enough for businesses to remain confident their operations will continue producing returns. What reasonable leader can repeatedly increase the cost of doing business in a state and then express surprise when businesses leave? Simply put, unless you are on welfare, a drug tourist , homeless, live in a gated and privately protected neighborhood, or a California politician who flies in for a photo opportunity and promptly leaves, the California model no longer works.
California’s leaders have spent years showing us the results of their policies. This election season, voters should send the message that these ideas don’t work.

Chad Hagan is a financier, author, executive producer, and philanthropist involved in economic and environmental policy in the United States and United Kingdom. He is the author of the book “The Myth of California: How Big Government Destroyed the Golden State.”

articles.headline: TextNow’s $150 Moto G Play Is Customized for Kids and Pairs Up With a $20 Monthly Plan
keyFacts: TextNow is launching Yello on Tuesday, a child-friendly Moto G Play phone priced at $150 with a $20 monthly plan.
The Android phone restricts app downloads and limits communication to parent-approved contacts managed through a web-based portal.
The device aims to limit distractions and inappropriate content while allowing kids to make calls, send texts, and share photos with parents.
body: Low-cost carrier TextNow is launching its first child-friendly phone on Tuesday, pairing a heavily discounted Motorola handset with a software portal that lets parents control who their kid can call or text.

Yello is a customized Moto G Play that costs $150 — $100 less than the standard model’s current retail price — and comes with a $20 monthly plan, with no other required contracts or service commitments.

The Android phone restricts access to Google’s Play Store and doesn’t allow users to install additional apps or services. It’s designed primarily for calls and texts with parent-approved contacts, which parents can manage through a web-based portal that also lets them check the phone’s GPS location. Kids can call or text those contacts from a menu of large icons reminiscent of Netflix’s profile selection screen.
More from CNET

Other software available on the phone includes access to the cameras — a 32-megapixel main camera and an 8-megapixel front-facing camera — along with the calculator, clock and a weather app. Seven preloaded games can be enabled, which include phone classics such as Snake, Mines and Tic-Tac-Toe. Photos taken on the phone can only be shared with parents.

This more restrictive approach should let kids stay in touch with approved friends and coordinate pickups with parents while limiting distractions and access to content inappropriate for young children.

The 2026 Moto G Play is a good choice for Yello’s software approach. When I reviewed the phone last year, I liked its larger 5,200-mAh battery because it could easily get through two days of use. But its less-powerful processor, 64GB of storage and 4GB of memory made it challenging to use as a media machine. Since Yello’s software deliberately avoids that use, the Moto G Play should be more than sufficient for calls and texts.
Despite the name, the Yello phone is available in just one color: the same soft blue on every 2026 Moto G Play that Motorola calls “pantone tapestry.”

Most US carriers offer their own versions of child-friendly devices such as Yello. AT&T, for instance, has repurposed the Samsung Galaxy A16 into the AmiGo Jr with similar parental controls. There are also a number of child-friendly smartwatches, which may be a better option depending on your family’s needs for connectivity. But Yello does offer a lot of flexibility, since it doesn’t require a more expensive unlimited data plan or a minimum service commitment.

articles.headline: DOJ sends grand jury subpoenas to Philadelphia DA Krasner after judge's referral, sources say
keyFacts: The Justice Department issued grand jury subpoenas to Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner's office regarding potential obstruction of justice, sources said.
The subpoenas followed a federal judge's referral of Krasner and his top deputy for a possible criminal investigation over a murder conviction case.
Neither Krasner nor his deputy has been charged with any crimes.
body: The Justice Department sent grand jury subpoenas to Democratic Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner's office in recent days, Fox News has learned.

Two sources briefed on the subpoenas say they are related to potential obstruction of justice relating to the handling of cases before federal judges. The sources said the subpoenas came as a result of a federal judge referring Krasner and his top deputy to the DOJ for possible criminal investigation.
Krasner's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The DOJ declined to comment.
FEDERAL JUDGE REFERS PHILADELPHIA DA LARRY KRASNER TO DOJ FOR POSSIBLE CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION

Reports of the subpoenas come more than a month after U.S. District Judge Paul Diamond referred Krasner and his deputy, Matthew Stiegler, to the DOJ, saying evidence uncovered in a murder conviction case could constitute false statements, perjury, obstruction of justice and conspiracy.
Neither man has been charged.
DELETED EMAIL DETAILS ALLEGED TRUMP-TARGETING PUSH INSIDE LETITIA JAMES’ OFFICE: ‘FIND AND PURSUE CRIMES’
Diamond also disqualified Krasner and Stiegler from the case but declined to disqualify the entire DA's office.

The judge alleged that Krasner and Stiegler sought to pressure prosecutors into presenting a false narrative to the court and that Krasner warned of "consequences" if staff alerted the court to an internal conflict.
BIDEN-ERA FEDERAL PROSECUTOR HIT WITH CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION REFERRAL OVER ALLEGED FALSE STATEMENTS TO FBI
"I have thus reluctantly concluded that Philadelphia’s highest law enforcement official and one of his top assistants may have violated the law," Diamond wrote.
The dispute stems from the case of Dennis Johnson, who was convicted in 2009 of killing Kenyatta Smith.
SOROS NETWORK REBUILDS PROGRESSIVE PROSECUTOR PUSH AFTER STRING OF ELECTION LOSSES
The DA’s office said in a 2022 filing that Johnson was entitled to habeas corpus relief based on ineffective assistance of counsel, according to The Associated Press .
Prosecutors later raised potential conflicts involving Stiegler and urged that the matter be referred to the Pennsylvania Attorney General’s Office .
PHILADELPHIA DA SAYS HE'LL KEEP PIECE OF TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM 'AFTER WE ALL BLOW IT UP'
According to the opinion, Krasner opposed that move and repeatedly said someone from his office needed to remain involved to "protect the office."

"I respectfully and vigorously disagree with the court’s findings of fact and conclusions of law," Krasner said in a statement at the time. "I look forward to appealing to the higher court as soon as the law allows. This remains a pending matter, which limits for now my and my office’s ability to respond in the media."

articles.headline: Amnesia: The Dark Descent's co-founder explained the 'the dynamic of Steam' to Red Barrels after Outlast's sales slowed down
keyFacts: Frictional Games co-founder Thomas Grip advised Red Barrels co-founder Morin on Steam sales dynamics after Outlast sales slowed down.
Amnesia: The Dark Descent served as an inspiration for Red Barrels by proving there was an open market for their game.
Outlast ultimately achieved its sales goals and generated enough revenue to pay significant bonuses to the development team.
body: Three of the most influential games from my childhood were Pokémon HeartGold, Amnesia: The Dark Descent, and Outlast. Knowing this, you could probably piece together the kind of person I have become—let's just say it explains a lot. So it brought a smile to my face when I learned that without one of these influential games, I wouldn't have had the other—no, Pokémon HeartGold has nothing to do with anything—it's actually Amnesia which helped bring Outlast to the world.

Red Barrels, the Outlast devs, already discussed how difficult it was to pitch Outlast to publishers in an interview with GameSpot. But they also mentioned how Amnesia: The Dark Descent was something of a lodestar for the team.

Not only did the success of Amnesia reassure Red Barrels that there was in fact a market for the kind of game they were trying to make, but the fact that no one else had really tried to ride its coattails meant there was a space left wide open for them.

Some of the Red Barrels devs even sat in on a conference talk where Frictional Games co-founder Thomas Grip revealed that Amnesia: The Dark Descent sold an impressive 400,000 copies in its first year. This quickly became Outlast's goalpost.

But when sales for Outlast began to die down, Red Barrels co-founder Morin decided to reach out to Grip for some advice in how to navigate the changing tides of Steam: “He explained to us the dynamic of Steam, and when you do promotion, it spikes back up, [then] goes back down, and basically your sales curve becomes like a roller coaster.”

Everything worked out in the end thankfully. With Outlast going on to meet its initial target and earning enough money to pay the team "pretty significant bonuses". The Outlast series would eventually smash that target, selling millions of copies with its Whistleblower DLC, sequel, and multiplayer game all proving successful in their own right.

articles.headline: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
keyFacts: Security researchers reported Monday that Meta AI's Muse agent exposes sensitive personal and business information when users share conversations via web links.
Researchers from Claroc discovered they could easily find 6,800 share links because the URLs include conversation titles and use a specific domain name.
The exposed links contained confidential materials such as executive search notes, internal revenue reviews, loan applications, and staff vacation calendars.
body: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through Web links, researchers reported Monday.

Like many online services, Muse allows users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.
A single query is all that’s required

Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including:
- a candidate’s notes preparing for a confidential executive-search call with a frontier AI lab, naming the lab’s internal contact and the meeting time
- a national marketing company’s internal revenue review, marked for its CEO
- a small-business owner’s loan application, with the amount requested
- a to-do list that included a bank fraud alert, with a partial account number and a transaction amount and time
- a real-estate investor’s internal performance report, with two property addresses and exact return, income, and mortgage figures
- a workplace’s full-year staff vacation calendar, listing dozens of employees against the week each one would be away
“If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.”

The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database.

Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design to include the conversation title in the URL decision that makes the public discovery possible.

articles.headline: UK asks Apple to widen access to its payment tech
keyFacts: The Competition and Markets Authority wants Apple to widen access to its contactless payment technology and substantially lower its fees.
The watchdog argued that Apple's current rules and charges are blocking fintech firms from innovating and growing in the UK.
Apple stated that widening access could undermine user privacy and security protections.
body: - Published
UK smartphone users could benefit from new payment, ticket and travel apps if Apple widens access to its contactless payment tech, the competition watchdog says.
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) also wants the fees Apple charges firms to use its contactless tech to be "substantially lower".

It believes the iPhone maker's current fees and charges are "blocking" financial technology firms and others from innovating and growing - and is consulting on proposals it believes would cause these fees to fall.
Apple maintains that widening access could undermine security, and that its current arrangements do not stop innovation.
Nearly 2 in 5 payments are now contactless, the watchdog said, with nearly 60% of people using digital wallets - with Apple's the most popular in the UK.

In a statement Apple told the BBC that the current arrangements had permitted developers in the UK and around the world to securely offer contactless transactions directly within their apps, for everything from in-store payments and transit passes to car keys and event tickets.

"This solution enables developers and banks to create innovative products and services for their customers and facilitates competition between wallets, while ensuring users' sensitive data remains protected by the highest security standards".

"We do not believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an approach with lower privacy and security protections. We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome that is in the best interest of our users."
Last year Apple warned UK regulators against following the same path as the EU which forced it to open up a range of its technologies to rivals.
However, the CMA argued that, unlike the EU, it is focused on ensuring the interoperability of particular aspects of Apple's tech, such as digital wallets and watches.

The proposed measures would force Apple to grant access to apps that make payments via a widely used alternative contactless technology standard, called Host Card Emulation (HCE), which the firm does not currently permit in the UK.
New wallets, IDs and digital keys
The UK is one of the world's leading fintech hubs, the CMA said, generating more than Â£214 billion in turnover and supporting more than 360,000 jobs.
But Apple's fees and rules contactless payments are restricting growth and innovation, it argued.
Changes could enable the development of a wide range of new products, such as account-to-account payments, digital IDs, travel passes and digital keys, it claimed.
The regulator said moves to open up the tech in the EU had resulted in the creation of new businesses.
In the six months since the EU forced Apple to widen access to its tech, an alternative payment app Vipps launched, followed by PayPal, Klarna, Curve, and BBVA.
Apple argues however that the these new apps could easily have been launched prior to the changes.
But in the UK not a single firm has launched a wallet-type product to compete with Apple's the watchdog argued.
The CMA said it was not proposing to set the price and terms Apple could demand for use of its devices contactless tech, but the effect of its plans would be that prices would fall.

Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the CMA said it had been told that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple's contactless technology made it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete.
"By removing barriers to entry, we can help create the conditions for brilliant British businesses with great ideas to develop new products and services," she said.

articles.headline: Ronaldo let Manchester United down - Ten Hag
keyFacts: Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag stated that Cristiano Ronaldo let the team and him down during his tenure at Old Trafford.
Ten Hag said Ronaldo failed to properly prepare his fitness and did not work for the team during matches.
Ronaldo left the club in controversial circumstances after an unauthorized interview in November 2022 where he said he felt betrayed.
body: - Published
Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag said Cristiano Ronaldo "let the team and let me down" during the Dutchman's spell at Old Trafford.
Portugal forward Ronaldo was in his second spell at United when Ten Hag took charge in the summer of 2022 but left in controversial circumstances a few months later.
"He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him," Ten Hag told The Athletic, external.
"I flew out to Portugal to speak with him about what I was aiming for before I came to United.
"Obviously, he's one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in."
Ten Hag had dropped Ronaldo for a Premier League game at Chelsea in October 2022 after he had refused to come on as a substitute against Tottenham three days earlier.
Ronaldo gave an interview in the November in which he said he felt "betrayed" by United, did not respect Ten Hag and was being forced out of the club prior to his departure being "mutually agreed".
Ronaldo was 36 when he returned to Manchester United from Juventus in 2021, when Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was manager.
Under Ten Hag, he scored just three goals in 16 outings before his exit during the 2022-23 campaign.

"It's the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he's exhausted," added Ten Hag. "But he couldn't. He ran neither in possession nor out of possession. The reason was because he didn't prepare himself.
"Every top team has to embrace the top player, but the top player has to work for the team.

"He was telling the players, 'save your legs at the training'. I understand it when you are top fit - you have sessions you can save the legs. But first you have to train yourself to get into the right fitness levels."

The publication of Ten Hag's interview comes as Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension and fined 255 euros (Â£215) by the Portuguese Football Federation for leaving his country's international camp last month.
Ten Hag was sacked by Manchester United in October 2024, having won the Carabao Cup in 2023 and FA Cup in 2024.
On his time at Old Trafford, Ten Hag added he wanted to sign Frenkie de Jong, Harry Kane and Declan Rice, and was against the sale of Scott McTominay to Napoli in August 2024.

"I said for the first season, 'centre-half, there's a problem, centre-midfield, there is a problem, and especially I need a strategist, then we need goals'. And that was the biggest issue in all my three years: goals," said Ten Hag.

articles.headline: The latest game event to fall afoul of US visa rules is a live concert for horse girl racer Umamusume: Pretty Derby
keyFacts: Developers Cygames cancelled the Los Angeles stop of the Umamusume: Pretty Derby live concert tour because they could not obtain the necessary US entry visas.
Cygames stated that they worked with lawyers and promoters for over six months to try and secure the visas before cancelling the event.
The cancellation follows similar recent issues with US visa approvals affecting other game-related events and performers in California.
body: Umamusume: Pretty Derby has turned out to be one of the most popular games in the world, partly due to being a gacha game and partly due to making pretty girls out of very real Japanese racehorses (which introduces a unique mourning when the real horse passes away and the anime girl lives on). A new kind of mourning faces the Umamusume fanbase now, as an upcoming stop on the game's The Stage: World Tour at Los Angeles' Peacock Theater has been cancelled right before it was supposed to open this week. The apparent cause? The US visa system.

First announced in July, the concert was supposed to begin on Wednesday, but developers Cygames have unfortunately had to confirm that it cannot run as planned. The reason for this is stated to be that "although we have coordinated repeatedly with all parties concerned and explored every possible option in our efforts to make this event happen, we were unable to obtain the necessary visas for entry into the US." In a prior post, they stated that they had been working with lawyers and promoters to acquire visas for "over six months", but had yet to receive a response.

This isn't the only recent example of a Los Angeles game concert being affected by struggles to obtain US visas, as a performer on Wuthering Waves' tour, Tarokiki, was also unable to perform in California due to not acquiring a visa in time. And it certainly isn't the first time that game events, more generally, have been affected by the US's increasingly outsider-hostile political climate. This year's GDC quite infamously saw a large number of international and/or queer developers elect not to attend, to prioritise their own safety.

The prospect of not being able to see the voices behind the horses in the flesh, nor to enjoy the soundtrack live in concert, seems to have been a sort of breaking point for some in the fanbase, as there have been quite a few posts from fans along the Community-esque lines of "I can excuse fascism, but I draw the line at cancelling the horse concert." One much-joked about poster stated, seemingly quite earnestly, "This will actually radicalize me if this gets cancelled, fuck my country." It is insane to think that there are genuinely people who might have begun to hop off an alt-right pipeline and learn class/cultural consciousness as a result of an Umamusume concert, but that's the world we live in. Everyone has a breaking point, I suppose; if it takes some people being affected by losing their precious treats to be radicalised against fascism, I'll take it as better than not being radicalised at all.

articles.headline: Over 300K visas revoked so far in Trump’s second term, State Department announces
keyFacts: The Trump administration has revoked more than 300,000 visas since taking office last year, according to the State Department.
A State Department official said the revocations targeted individuals involved in criminal activity, public safety threats, or immigration fraud.
State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott stated that the administration has revoked more visas at a faster pace than any administration in history.
body: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration has revoked more than 300,000 visas since the 47th president took office last year, The Post has learned.
A State Department official said that the revocations were done as a consequence for criminal activity, threats to public safety or immigration violations such as fraud or misrepresentation.
At least 4,000 visas were yanked from foreign nationals “who engage in or facilitated birth tourism,” the official noted.
“With over 300,000 revocations, the Trump administration has revoked more visas at a faster pace than any administration in history,” added State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott.

“Let the message be clear: we have zero tolerance for foreigners here on visas who break the law, commit fraud, or undermine our national security. We are taking, and will continue to take, action to keep our borders, and our nation, secure.”
The nationalities of those who had their visa revoked was not immediately clear.
Last month, the department had confirmed as many as 250,000 revocations had taken place since January 2025.
The pace of revocations has accelerated so far in 2026 after just 23,000 cases were vetted by the Bureau of Consular Affairs last year.
A quarter of visas pulled in 2025 were for assaults or related crimes, while another 22% were yanked for driving under the influence, 7% for theft and 7% for substance abuse or distribution.

articles.headline: Bestselling Author and Economic Commentator Kyla Scanlon Launches Weekly Podcast, ‘Best of Luck,’ with Vox
keyFacts: Author Kyla Scanlon and Vox announced a new weekly video interview podcast titled Best of Luck.
The show features interviews with diverse guests to provide career guidance tied to the modern economy.
The podcast premieres on October 27, with new episodes releasing weekly on Tuesdays.
body: Kyla Scanlon, New York Times bestselling author and economic commentator, and Vox today announced the launch of Best of Luck, a new weekly video interview podcast premiering October 27. Each week, Scanlon will sit down with guests who have something to teach us about how to build a meaningful career in this uncertain moment, from economists to journalists, farmers to comedians. They’ll share their most instructive detours, setbacks, and successes, and Scanlon will tie each story back to the economy that we’re all living in, with takeaways for anyone at any stage of their working life.
Bestselling Author and Economic Commentator Kyla Scanlon Launches Weekly Podcast, ‘Best of Luck,’ with Vox
Premiering October 27, the weekly video podcast is a guide to building a meaningful career at any age in an economy where the traditional playbook no longer applies.

“So much of the advice we are given about building a career still comes from an economy that doesn’t really exist anymore,” Scanlon said. “There is no one right way to build a career, especially now. The goal of this show is to ask guests how they actually did it, across the best parts, the worst parts, and the parts that were lucky. Then we put it to work! Every guest sits for a mock job interview and does an advice autopsy, and we talk about how you build your own luck. Hearing how other people found their path can help all of us make better decisions about our own.”

Named to the Time 100’s Creators list and Barron’s 100 Most Influential Women in Finance, Scanlon has emerged as one of the most distinct voices making economics make sense for everyone, especially a new generation. Known for breaking down complex economic ideas and connecting them to the realities of everyday life, she coined the term “vibecession” to describe the disconnect between economic data and how people actually feel about the economy. She is the author of the New York Times bestseller In This Economy? How Money & Markets Really Work, a CNN contributor and analyst, and a monthly New York Times Opinion contributor.

“At Vox, we have long been fans of Kyla’s work — her approach to explaining the economy in an accessible, approachable way really personifies Vox’s explanatory approach,” said Swati Sharma, editor-in-chief and publisher at Vox. “With this new show, we’re thrilled for her to help our audience understand how to navigate work and careers in this economy so they can live more meaningful lives.”

“Kyla has a gift for translating the big, confusing picture of our economy into what it means for each of us,” said Lillian Xu, vice president of podcast business at Vox Media. “With Best of Luck, she’s doing the same for a job market that keeps changing the rules, in conversations with experts that are practical and honest about how careers really unfold today. We’re so excited to partner with her to help more people figure out what’s next.”
The trailer for Best of Luck is out today, with the first episode coming on October 27 and new episodes following weekly on Tuesdays.

At Vox, Best of Luck joins a stable of popular podcasts including Today, Explained, The Gray Area, and America, Actually. Vox’s shows are part of the Vox Media Podcast Network, one of the largest US podcast publishers and home to some of the most influential talent across categories, including journalist Kara Swisher and entrepreneur Scott Galloway (hosts of Pivot), tennis champion Maria Sharapova (host of Pretty Tough), former Manhattan US Attorney Preet Bharara (host of Stay Tuned), basketball legend Sue Bird (host of Bird’s Eye View), and more. Vox Media will oversee production, sales, marketing, and distribution for Best of Luck, which joins a dynamic slate of shows that shape conversations across business, culture, and beyond.
About Kyla Scanlon

Kyla Scanlon is the founder of Kyla Labs. She writes about money, markets, and the systems that shape them for an audience of over 1 million people across TikTok, Instagram, Substack, and YouTube, covering the pressing issues of the day — including tariffs, artificial intelligence, energy markets, and why the traditional rungs of the economic ladder have gotten harder to climb. Her debut book, In This Economy? How Money & Markets Really Work, was a New York Times bestseller and used hand-drawn diagrams to make the machinery of the economy clear. In her newsletter, she coined the term “vibecession” to describe the disconnect between strong economic data and negative public sentiment — a concept since referenced by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and taken up in research by former CEA chair Jared Bernstein.

Raised in Kentucky, Scanlon studied finance, economics, and data analytics at Western Kentucky University. She started out trading options and selling cars, where she first saw how inaccessible finance had become to the people it affected most. She began making whiteboard videos and comedy skits to decode markets and economic trends for everyday audiences (and often dressed up as Jerome Powell). She writes monthly for New York Times Opinion, has a video partnership with Foreign Policy, and is a contributor and analyst at CNN. She is also a senior fellow at the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator and a research fellow at the American Institute for Boys and Men. Scanlon was named to Barron’s 100 Most Influential Women in US Finance and the Time 100 Creators list, and has appeared on The Daily Show with Jon Stewart and The Ezra Klein Show. At work on her second book, she lives in the mountains with her dog, Piglet.
About Vox

Vox was launched in 2014 to address the disconnect between the widely reported facts of the day and a true understanding of why something happened. It developed a widely imitated explainer format that delivers understanding across digital platforms, newsletters, a YouTube channel with nearly 13 million subscribers, and a stable of podcasts. Under the leadership of Editor-in-Chief Swati Sharma, Vox has grown a membership programs with tens of thousands of paying subscribers.
About the Vox Media Podcast Network

The Vox Media Podcast Network is one of the largest US podcast publishers and home to some of the most popular and influential shows. Reaching a monthly audience of tens of millions across audio, video, and social platforms, its podcasts spark conversations, frame issues, and define the popular zeitgeist across politics, technology, business, sports, entertainment, and more. Learn more at podcasts.voxmedia.com.

articles.headline: DOJ charges 28 with voting crimes. And, TikTok ignored staff's child safety concerns
keyFacts: The Justice Department charged 28 green card holders in California with election crimes for allegedly registering or voting illegally.
Court records show TikTok employees repeatedly warned leadership about child safety risks, including sexual exploitation and suicide content.
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists updated its menopause treatment guidelines to recommend hormone replacement therapy.
body: DOJ charges 28 with voting crimes. And, TikTok ignored staff's child safety concerns
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories

The Justice Department has charged 28 green card holders in California with election crimes for allegedly illegally registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections. This marks a significant escalation in the Trump administration's feud with the state over its voting system as the midterm elections approach. The DOJ also filed an emergency request to prevent California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls that the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." California has sought clarification on the federal government's conclusions but has not received any. Last week, the DOJ sued California and Los Angeles County after local officials refused to investigate allegations made by the administration about noncitizen voting.

- 🎧 The DOJ wants California to segregate ballots of those on its list and to delay counting them until investigations are complete. Election law experts doubt the DOJ will succeed, given its past attempts to change state voting processes, Miles Parks tells Up First. He adds that it would be surprising to see a shift just two weeks before the election with ballots already distributed. Research shows that in many cases, when legal permanent residents register to vote, it is due to a misunderstanding of the rules. Experts tell Parks they are concerned that federal law enforcement might use accusations to confiscate ballots during counting, but many local voting officials are preparing by keeping county attorneys on speed dial.

Democrats and Republicans are deciding which races to prioritize with Election Day just two weeks away. President Trump is campaigning in key perennial purple states like Georgia, North Carolina, Kansas, Iowa and Florida this week.

- 🎧 Trump's rally in Kansas and trip to North Carolina aren't where the leader of the Republican Party's attention should be, NPR's Stephen Fowler says. Kansas hasn't elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, and many Republican groups have ceased ad spending in North Carolina, viewing the Senate race as a lost cause. Republicans are prioritizing efforts to save their Senate majority over saving the House majority, while Democrats are capitalizing on opportunities in conservative areas, Fowler says. In Georgia, with a million voters already casting ballots, Fowler says he sees an increase in Black voter turnout in the state and across the South.

- ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

TikTok employees repeatedly raised concerns about the app's risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide content. Previously unreported court records show employees' frustration with leadership's response to these issues. Depositions filed in March 2026 provide new insights into TikTok's child safety measures since its surge in popularity in 2018. Staff alerted management about minors engaging with sexual content, which the company profited from. They also identified loopholes that allowed users under 18 to bypass age restrictions and block parental oversight of their app activity. The records show that TikTok avoided conducting age surveys, fearing it would have to share results with the Federal Trade Commission.
Life advice

Cold and flu season in the U.S. starts this month and lasts through May, according ot the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Cooler temperatures and drier air can increase our vulnerability to illnesses like the common cold, flu, RSV and COVID-19. Get ahead of the game now by putting together a cold-and-flu prep kit. Here's what experts say you should have in your home.

- 🤒 Over-the-counter medications are good options, but always follow the recommended dosage to avoid risks or side effects. Some good medications to have include ibuprofen or naproxen, which can relieve headaches, body aches and sore throats by reducing inflammation and Acetaminophen, which can lower body temperature.

- 🤒 Honey acts as an anti-inflammatory and soothes the throat, making it useful for young children who can't take cough medicine. But don't give it to children under 12 months due to the risk of botulism.
- 🤒 A thermometer is a must-have for checking your temperature. For children 3 and under, a rectal option is preferred.
- 🤒 A saline spray or rinse for your nose can help keep the mucous membranes moist and help relieve symptoms by loosening thick mucus during a cold.

For more advice on how to stock your medicine cabinet for cold and flu season, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.
Picture show

Pleasant Rowland launched Pleasant Company in 1986 with three dolls — Samantha, Molly and Kirsten — creating an empire known as American Girl. To celebrate its 40th anniversary, author Fiona Davis was asked to write a historical fiction book for adults titled Samantha: The Next Chapter, featuring Samantha Parkington, who has turned 25. The story picks up after Samantha's last book, in which she attended a suffragist rally with her aunt Cornelia. The book is set 15 years later, in 1920, just after the ratification of the 19th Amendment. Samantha learns that her grandmother's inheritance has been stolen, forcing her to transition from socialite to shopgirl overnight. NPR's Samantha Balaban visited the American Girl store in New York with her own Samantha doll to explore the character's evolution over the years, drawing on insights from its staff and Davis. Check out photos from the visit and read more about the history of American Girl dolls.
3 things to know before you go

- The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its menopause treatment guidelines for the first time since 2014. The group now recommends using hormone replacement therapy along with some other treatments to alleviate symptoms.
- A wedding day can be one of the costliest days in a couple's life. Some are opting to save money by choosing grocery-store cakes over specialty bakers' cakes.

- Vegemite is such an iconic breakfast spread in Australia that a convicted killer is suing the state of Victoria for the right to eat it in prison. The state has banned Vegemite because it could potentially be used to brew alcohol and throw off dogs.

articles.headline: Zelenskyy meets with Trump envoys as U.S. blasts ‘scandalous’ accusations on withdrawn support
keyFacts: U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday.
Ukraine accused the U.S. of withdrawing crucial defense support and withholding intelligence, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio called scandalous and inaccurate.
Rubio stated that nothing has changed in U.S. support and that missile interceptor shortages are due to balancing obligations rather than denial.
body: U.S. envoys were expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambles to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.

President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have so far had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war. Their latest meeting comes with Washington’s backing in doubt as Kyiv accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to its defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.”

Witkoff will be meeting with Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, with Kushner joining via videoconference, the Norwegian government said. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb will also join the talks, it added.

Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters he hoped that it would be possible for Trump’s envoys to hold a meeting in Russia “in the near future,” though he gave no firm indication on when this might be.

Trump has waived sanctions and agreed a diesel deal with Russia, in an apparent bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the Midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate,” his latest rebuke of the Ukrainian president.
Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.”
It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine.
Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles on Sunday, the third time in recent days.

In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the SpaceX service, with no explanation from the American side.

“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan Congressional delegation. He also said the U.S. was delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors, and that Ukraine has nearly run out of its supplies.

Zelenskyy said early Tuesday he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.”
Rubio told reporters later that he told Zelenskyy in the 45-minute call that nothing had changed in U.S. support for Ukraine.
“There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he added, speaking at the start of a trip to India.

When it comes to missile interceptors, Rubio said the U.S. has to strike a delicate balance between its obligations to other partners and its own requirements when it comes to what he called “the most in-demand product” in the defense industry right now.
“When a country doesn’t get interceptors from the United States, it’s not because we are denying,” he added. “We have our own needs too.”

Ukrainian officials including Zelenskyy have made clear their accusation that the U.S. has imposed restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks more deadly.
“That’s scandalous, that’s outrageous, that’s just simply not true. That’s not accurate,” Rubio said Tuesday.

Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a one-year-old girl they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region.

articles.headline: Erik ten Hag accuses Cristiano Ronaldo of ‘letting down’ Manchester United
keyFacts: Erik ten Hag stated that Cristiano Ronaldo let Manchester United down and refused to follow tactical instructions during their time together.
Ten Hag alleged that club owners failed to keep promises regarding support and communication, leading to his sacking in October 2024.
Ten Hag expressed disappointment and embarrassment when the club sold Scott McTominay without his consent.
body: Erik ten Hag has claimed Cristiano Ronaldo “let the team down” during their time together at Manchester United. Ten Hag has also alleged that promises made by United’s owners went unfulfilled, leading to his sacking by the club in October 2024.

Ronaldo returned for a second spell at United in August 2021 and was already at the club when Ten Hag was appointed in April 2022 as Ole Gunnar Solskjær’s successor. The relationship between the pair quickly broke down, however, with Ronaldo refusing to come on as a substitute in a win against Tottenham in October 2022 before he then publicly criticised the club in a TV interview. The forward’s contract was mutually terminated the following month.

“He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him,” Ten Hag said in an interview with the Athletic. “He’s one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in.”

Ten Hag claims Ronaldo did not complete the full run that players were set after they were beaten 4-0 by Brentford early in his reign. “I confronted him with this,” Ten Hag said. “Many times I say: ‘Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can’t bring yourself in the box, you can’t score.’”

Ten Hag was sacked only five months after he won the FA Cup and then signed a contract extension. The Dutchman claimed in the discussions with the club’s owners about his new deal that he was made promises which were not kept, and he was left “embarrassed” when Scott McTominay was sold to Napoli without his consent. He said: “They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned. We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn’t keep.
“I said: ‘No selling Scott McTominay.’ And in the end they sold him. I got, of course, very embarrassed and disappointed.”
